title: Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio
detail:
Global stocks move upward despite shock warning from Panmure Liberum analyst who sold all equities in his personal portfolio
Jim Edwards
Thu, November 26, 2026 at 11:47 AM EST 4 min read
^GSPC
^NDX
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

With America offline for Thanksgiving, the rest of the world enjoyed a break from the market chaos caused by U.S. tariff policy, U.S. AI investment, and U.S. interest rate rises.

In Asia, stocks broadly rose. Europe was up strongly. And although New York was closed for the holiday, S&P 500 futures were up.

Nasdaq 100 futures were up 0.63%, and Nvidia was up 1.29% in after-market trading.

None of this should be happening!

There is nothing but bad news on the horizon, multiple Wall Street and London City analysts said in emails to Fortune.

The most dramatic warning came from Panmure Liberum's Joachim Klement (who writes a well-regarded Substack on investing whose subtitle is "Thoughts on financial markets by a grumpy, middle-aged German. What more do you want?")

He gave a video talk in which he announced he was selling all the equities—all of them!—in his personal investment portfolio because of the recent selloff in the S&P 500: "I think that we are heading towards a major bear market with more than 30% drawdown risk." His official forecast for 2027 is that the S&P 500 will sink to 5,000—a level that right now seems unthinkable. His concern is that the index is currently trading below its 200-day moving average: "As Paul Tudor Jones the famous investor once said, nothing good happens below the 200-day moving average."

"It doesn't look like the Santa Claus rally is in store for us this year"

Three factors are driving the gloom:

Firstly, inflation is still too high. The Fed's preferred metric, the index for personal consumption expenditures, was up year-over-year to 3.8% in October, up from 3.7% the month before. "Undesirably strong," as Lawrence Werther and Brendan Stuart of Daiwa Capital Markets said in a note. That will almost certainly push the Fed into raising interest rates in December in order to make money more scarce—a scenario that generally augurs poorly for stocks.

Many analysts pointed to a speech given Monday by John Williams, the President of the New York Fed. He all but telegraphed that the Fed was going to kick the rate up soon: "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2 percent goal in a timely manner and on a sustained basis. There is still work to do to get that done." (There is a good analysis of the speech by economist Claudia Sahm here.)

Secondly, the U.S. economy is strong, so the Fed will feel it has the breathing space to dampen inflationary demand.

New jobless claims came in near their three-year low, and the long-term trend in jobless claims continues to point down, according to Thomas Simons and Blake Birkins of Jefferies.

Key Takeaways

Walmart stock is up 10% in the past month while the Nasdaq 100 fell 11%, as investors moved out of tech and into consumer names like Home Depot and Dollar Tree.

Michael Burry calls Walmart one of the market's "generals." These are the stocks investors hold longest in a selloff, and after the 2000 and 2007 peaks they held up for months before falling too.

Walmart's third quarter beat its own guidance and it raised its full-year outlook, though Target grew comparable sales faster.

At about 43x forward earnings, against a five-year average near 30x, Walmart looks like a hold until the price comes down.

Walmart (WMT:NASDAQ) stock is up 10% in the past month, while the S&P 500 fell 6% and the Nasdaq 100 fell 11%. Money leaving tech poured into the chains Americans shop at every week, from Home Depot (HD:NYSE) and Dollar Tree (DLTR:NASDAQ) to Target (TGT:NYSE).

Michael Burry has noticed. On Cassandra Unchained, the blog he now writes, he put Walmart alongside Apple and Costco as the market's "generals": "The tech leaders have now joined in the fun. The generals are still standing. It may be a few months before we know."

Burry's generals are the familiar names investors hold after selling everything else. After the 2000 peak, they held up for six months. After 2007, seven to eight months. Then they fell too.

Some compliment.

It started with the midterms

The rotation took hold on Nov. 4, the day after Democrats won both houses of Congress. Walmart jumped that day, and Home Depot rose 7% as investors bet on housing-affordability policy and lower Treasury yields. Home Depot is up 13% over the past month, which is a big move for a company guiding to about 2% adjusted EPS growth this year. Then on Nov. 24, Dollar Tree reported third-quarter comparable sales up 4.6% on 3.8% more traffic, and its 11% jump lifted discount retailers into Black Friday.

Key Takeaways

Goldman Sachs fell 8% in the past week and hit a new 52-week low on Nov. 25 with no bad news of its own, as AI stocks sold off and markets priced in a near-certain December rate hike.

The drop came the same week Goldman and Apollo priced about $44 billion of notes to buy AI chips for SpaceX.

Analysts still expect Goldman's earnings to grow through 2028, and Morgan Stanley's latest quarter shows the trading boom is intact, so the selling looks overdone.

Goldman Sachs (GS:NYSE) fell 8% in the week to its Nov. 25 close of $801.03, after touching a new 52-week low of $772.74 that morning. The Nasdaq 100 fell 4% over the same stretch.

Goldman put out no bad news. But it had just helped arrange a giant AI chip financing for SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ), and a December Fed hike now looks all but certain, a worry it shares with rival Morgan Stanley (MS:NYSE).

Goldman became AI's banker at a bad time

On Nov. 20, Goldman and Apollo announced they had priced about $44 billion of notes to fund GPUs for SpaceX. AI stocks sold off hard that same day. That leaves a question TIKR raised on Nov. 21: how much of that debt Goldman kept on its own books.

SpaceX stock fell 11% over the same week. With third-quarter capex of $19.6 billion against $14.6 billion of revenue, it will likely keep borrowing, and that means more fees for Goldman as long as investors keep buying the debt.

A Fed hike would hit the deal business

On Nov. 25, October's core PCE inflation came in at 3.3%, above forecasts, and CME's FedWatch tool kept the odds of a December rate hike at about 97%. Stocks sank that morning before recovering most of the drop by the close. Higher rates make deals costlier to finance. Still, the latest results show no crack yet: Morgan Stanley's third-quarter equities revenue rose 41%, and Goldman's jumped 72%. Morgan Stanley reports on Jan. 14, and its trading line will show whether the boom outlasts a tighter Fed.

Key Takeaways

AT&T stock is up 10% in the past month as the broader market fell and investors moved into cheap, high-yielding stocks.

SpaceX wants to build a fourth US carrier, but the Boost Mobile network it wants to buy runs on AT&T and T-Mobile, which reportedly plan to cut it off.

AT&T's free cash flow covers its dividend more than twice over, and the stock trades at 9.0x forward earnings, right at its 5-year average.

Steve Eisman's "uninvestable" call looks too harsh on AT&T, though AST SpaceMobile's satellite rollout and fourth-quarter churn will show how the SpaceX fight plays out.

AT&T (T:NYSE) stock rose 10% in the month to its Nov. 25 close, while the S&P 500 fell 6% and the Nasdaq 100 fell 10%.

After the close on Oct. 22, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) was seeking access to at least 80,000 US cell sites to become a fourth carrier, and AT&T and T-Mobile US (TMUS:NASDAQ) each fell about 8% the next day. Since then, both have reportedly pushed back on SpaceX, and AT&T has leaned on its satellite partner, AST SpaceMobile (ASTS:NASDAQ).

Not everyone's buying the rebound. On the Nov. 6 episode of The Real Eisman Playbook, Steve Eisman said of AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile: "I think the big three are just uninvestable."

Income buyers came back

With no big company news, AT&T rode investors' move into steady, high-yielding stocks as tech sold off: Walmart rose 10%, McDonald's 14% and Campbell's more than 15% over the same stretch. Buyers had reason to like AT&T's third quarter. Adjusted EPS rose to $0.65 from $0.54 a year earlier, management raised its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to about $2.40 from $2.25-$2.35, and it kept its plan for $18 billion-plus of free cash flow. (Management credits most of that raise to halting depreciation on the Mexico unit it's selling.)

Analysts expect normalized EPS to keep rising, from $2.12 in 2025 to $2.93 in 2028:

title: The economy is hot, but stocks are not.

The economy is hot, but stocks are not.
Nathan Bomey
Wed, November 25, 2026 at 5:03 PM EST 2 min read
^NDX
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The economy is hot, but stocks are not.

Why it matters: Concerns about the sustainability of the AI spending binge have been looming over Wall Street for months — and those haven't gone away just because Jensen Huang is back on the job.

State of play: AI stocks were down in the dumps again Wednesday despite signs of a humming economy, as the feverish embrace of Huang's return to Nvidia fades.

New data Wednesday showed the U.S. economy grew at a 4.3% annual rate in the third quarter, powered by business investment — far above the 3.4% originally reported.

And rapid growth looks set to continue in the fourth quarter, according to the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow estimate, Axios' Neil Irwin writes.

But those good vibes weren't enough to stave off another tech-led risk-off move in markets.

Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index, which represents some of the biggest tech companies, was down as much as 4.7% Wednesday morning before closing down 0.6%.

It's now down nearly 12% since Huang was ousted (before he wasn't) at Nvidia.

Wednesday was another particularly ugly day for Nvidia, which closed down 3.9%.

The company has now shed nearly $1 trillion in market value since the Huang scandal broke and more than $2 trillion since its October peak.

Zoom in: The chip giant and center of the AI universe continues to face numerous unanswered questions surrounding the Huang episode.

And Wednesday, credit ratings firm S&P Global warned it may cut Nvidia's AA rating, citing concerns around its board's independence and "key man" risk.

Other AI stocks also swung between big losses and smaller ones Wednesday, with the chips sector and hyperscalers particularly volatile.

AMD, Micron, Intel and Marvell all pared far steeper losses before closing at 1.8%, 4.6%, 0.6% and 0.5%, respectively.

The Magnificent Seven were also feeling the pain Wednesday, with all but Meta and Apple trading down.

What they're saying: "We are not out of the woods with the downside risk from the AI trade, as the Jensen Huang stock put is fading," writes Chris Brigati, chief investment officer at San Antonio investment firm SWBC.

Investors are still nervous, he said. And fundamental questions about whether massive investments in AI will pay off remain unanswered.

Zoom out: Macro issues also contributed to Wednesday's stock volatility.

The federal government reported Wednesday that the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — rose 0.2% from September to 3.8% in October.

That likely heightens the chances of a Fed rate hike, putting additional pressure on growth stocks.

Looking ahead, I think the recent Broadcom sale could also prove costly after the company reports fourth-quarter earnings on Dec. 9.

Why I Think Wood Sold the Wrong Chip Stock

Broadcom expects Q4 revenue to grow 93% year-over-year (YOY) to $34.8 billion. The company's artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor revenue is expected to grow even more sharply by 236% to $21.7 billion. So, Broadcom's biggest business is guided to more than triple YOY.

CEO Hock Tan said that Broadcom has secured supply for about $115 billion in AI revenue in fiscal 2027 and a whopping $230 billion in fiscal 2028. The firm also expects EPS to be more than $30 by 2028. That's more than four times the $6.82 in non-GAAP EPS Broadcom earned in fiscal 2025. The company's custom chip deals run for years, which is why I've argued before that AVGO shouldn't be treated like every other AI chip stock.

The one area expected to get weaker in Q4 is gross margin, which management guided to approximately 73%, down from 78% a year ago. The projected drop is because its custom AI chips, which carry costly memory and earn lower margins, now make up a bigger share of sales. A weaker gross margin could give the bears something to point to.

Overall, though, I think most of the numbers look solid, while the valuation remains reasonable. If Dec. 9 confirms the guidance and the 2027 outlook holds, I think Ark Invest may come to regret selling AVGO stock when it did.
